Newborn Care

Cow’s milk protein allergy: recognising it and planning feeds

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Cow’s milk protein allergy happens when the immune system reacts to proteins in cow’s milk. It can affect formula-fed babies and, less commonly, babies reacting to small amounts of dietary protein reaching breast milk. It is different from lactose intolerance, which concerns digestion of milk sugar. A careful assessment matters because many ordinary infant symptoms resemble allergy.

Immediate and delayed reactions look different

An immediate, often IgE-mediated reaction can include hives, swelling, vomiting, wheeze or breathing difficulty shortly after exposure. A severe reaction can affect breathing or circulation and needs emergency treatment. Use prescribed adrenaline if indicated by your baby’s emergency plan and call emergency services.

Delayed, non-IgE-mediated reactions can cause gastrointestinal symptoms over a longer interval, such as blood or mucus in stools, ongoing diarrhoea, feeding difficulty or poor growth. These symptoms are not unique to milk allergy.

One important delayed pattern, called FPIES, can cause repeated vomiting with pallor and marked lethargy a few hours after a trigger. It may occur without hives or wheeze and can still be serious. Seek urgent care for that pattern rather than assuming delayed means mild.

Colic, reflux, gas or an unsettled evening alone does not prove allergy. Blood in a diaper or persistent vomiting deserves medical advice even when you suspect you know the cause.

How clinicians work out the diagnosis

A useful history includes the exact milk or food, amount, time to symptoms, what happened and whether it has happened again. Photographs of a rash and a brief feeding/symptom record can help. Growth and the baby’s general health are also important.

Skin-prick tests or specific-IgE blood tests can support the diagnosis of an immediate allergy when interpreted with the history. A positive result alone shows sensitisation and does not always establish a clinical allergy. Delayed allergy often has no useful routine blood or skin test.

For suspected delayed reactions, the team may recommend a short, defined exclusion trial followed by a planned reintroduction. Symptoms improving while milk is removed are not enough on their own, since infant symptoms can improve for other reasons.

Reintroduction is not always safe at home. Immediate reactions, severe reactions and FPIES may require specialist-supervised challenges. Do not use an internet milk ladder as a substitute for the diagnostic plan, and avoid unvalidated food-IgG panels or routine patch/stool testing as proof of milk allergy.

Mention relatives with eczema, asthma or food allergy as part of the history. A diary can include your own foods if symptoms seem linked to breastfeeding, without assuming every change proves a cause.

Breastfeeding can usually continue

A baby with cow’s milk allergy is not automatically allergic to breast milk. If your baby tolerates breastfeeding but reacts to formula, you may not need to remove dairy from your own diet. The decision depends on whether symptoms occur during breastfeeding itself.

When a maternal exclusion trial is appropriate, it commonly lasts two to four weeks and needs a clear review and reintroduction plan. Avoid removing dairy, soy, egg and multiple other foods all at once without guidance.

A dietitian can help replace calcium, vitamin D, protein and other nutrients if you need to avoid dairy. Read ingredient labels for milk proteins, including casein and whey, and review labels again when products change. Your team can explain how local allergen labelling and precautionary statements apply to the specific allergy.

There is no need to stop breastfeeding for a fixed two weeks to wait for milk proteins to disappear. Exposure and symptom recovery vary; continue with the feeding plan your clinician recommends.

If dairy exclusion is advised, ordinary milk, cheese, yoghurt, cream and butter are obvious sources. Less obvious milk ingredients may appear in chocolate, sauces and seasonings, processed meats, margarine and packaged meals. Check each label; a product category alone cannot tell you whether it contains milk.

Breastfeeding provides nutrition and infection protection. WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding for around six months, followed by complementary foods and continued breastfeeding to two years or beyond. These are population recommendations, not a guarantee against allergy or later illness, and families needing formula deserve practical support.

Choose a specialist formula when needed

If formula is required, an extensively hydrolysed formula is suitable for many babies with cow’s milk allergy. Although commonly made from cow’s milk, its proteins are broken down much more extensively than those in ordinary formula.

An amino-acid formula may be needed for severe disease, certain clinical circumstances or failure to tolerate an extensively hydrolysed product. The choice should account for symptoms, growth and specialist advice rather than marketing claims.

Partially hydrolysed comfort formula, ordinary lactose-free formula and goat’s-milk formula are not reliable substitutes for treating cow’s milk protein allergy. Removing lactose does not remove milk proteins, and proteins in other mammalian milks can cross-react.

Soy infant formula is an option only in selected circumstances; some babies also react to soy, and age and local guidance matter. Ordinary oat, almond or other plant drinks are not nutritionally complete infant formula. Never make a homemade substitute.

Specialist formulas can taste and smell different from ordinary formula. Ask the feeding team for help with acceptance rather than adding flavourings or switching back to an unsafe product.

Plan follow-up as your baby grows

Many children outgrow milk allergy, but timing varies by allergy type and individual history. Keep follow-up appointments to review growth, nutritional adequacy and when tolerance should be reassessed. Do not assume a birthday or a symptom-free period makes unsupervised exposure safe.

Before complementary feeding, ask which foods to avoid, which can be introduced normally and whether any introduction needs supervision. A milk allergy does not automatically require avoiding every other common allergen.

Make sure all caregivers know the feeding plan and, when relevant, the emergency plan. Appropriate formula, breastfeeding support and a focused diet can maintain nutrition while the diagnosis and longer-term outlook become clearer.

Having an unsettled baby can be exhausting. Family help, an allergy support group and a feeding professional can make the plan easier to follow. Genetic and family factors may influence allergy risk, but they do not determine whether an individual baby has an allergy.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Confirm suspected allergy with the clinical history and an appropriate exclusion and reintroduction plan; ordinary infant fussiness alone is not a diagnosis.

Support breastfeeding and growth, and choose specialist formula with professional advice when it is needed.

How BeMama can help

Keep a concise feed-and-symptom record and take it to your baby’s appointment; include questions about labels, nutrition and safe reassessment.

When to seek help

Breathing difficulty, collapse or severe lethargy after a feed needs emergency care. Repeated vomiting, blood in stools or poor growth needs prompt assessment.

Sources and further reading

  • Canadian Paediatric Society — Cow’s milk protein allergy in infants and children
  • WHO — Infant and young child feeding

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Milk-protein allergy is different from lactose intolerance.
  • Immediate and delayed reactions need different diagnostic approaches.
  • Breastfeeding usually continues; maternal dairy exclusion is not automatic.
  • Use an appropriate infant formula and a planned review of tolerance.

Frequently asked questions

Can a blood test diagnose every type of milk allergy?

No. Specific-IgE testing can help with immediate reactions, while delayed allergy is often assessed through the history and a structured exclusion/reintroduction plan.

Is lactose-free formula safe for milk allergy?

Ordinary lactose-free formula can still contain intact cow’s milk proteins. Ask for a formula intended for your baby’s diagnosed allergy.

Should I test milk again at home?

Only when the care team has explicitly planned a safe home reintroduction. Previous immediate or severe reactions may require supervised testing.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
